sections.title: Sorting and two-way external merge sort
sections.html:
Sorting requirements and external runs

ORDER BY requires order explicitly. DISTINCT, grouping, sort-merge joins, bulk index loading and RID-ordered fetches can also use sorting. For a compound key (A,B), compare A first and B only on equal A values: lexicographic order.

An external sort handles a file larger than its buffer budget by producing sorted runs and merging them. Ordinary in-memory quicksort over virtual memory gives no useful control over costly paging. A run is sorted internally even though separate runs are not yet ordered relative to one another.

PDF pp. 1–8

Two-way merge and every intermediate run

input pages: [3,4] [6,2] [9,4] [8,7] [5,6] [3,1] [2]
pass0 runs: [3,4] [2,6] [4,9] [7,8] [5,6] [1,3] [2]
pass1 runs: [2,3,4,6] [4,7,8,9] [1,3,5,6] [2]
pass2 runs: [2,3,4,4,6,7,8,9] [1,2,3,5,6]
pass3: [1,2,2,3,3,4,4,5,6,6,7,8,9]

Pass 0 sorts each page independently. Later passes merge two runs using two input buffers and one output buffer. Consume the smaller front tuple, refill an exhausted input page and flush a full output page. Seven input pages need 1+ceil(log₂7)=4 passes; if each pass materialises all seven pages, cost=2·7·4=56 I/Os. Duplicate values remain because this is sorting, not DISTINCT.

PDF pp. 9–10

sections.title: Multiway merge sort and index order
sections.html:
B-buffer sorting and the 108-page example

PassRunsRun lengths
02221×5 + 3
165×20 + 8
2280 + 28
31108

For B≥3, generate r₀=ceil(N/B) runs and repeatedly set rᵢ₊₁=ceil(rᵢ/(B−1)). One frame is reserved for merge output. For N=108,B=5 this gives 22→6→2→1: four passes, 864 I/Os. The recurrence handles ceilings and exact boundaries more reliably than floating logarithms. If N≤B, only initial sorting is needed; an empty input needs no data I/O. More buffers help by reducing initial runs and increasing merge fan-in, as the source plot shows.

PDF pp. 11–14

Can an index supply the required order?

Traverse to the first qualifying B+ leaf, then follow leaves in key order. Variant A directly yields records; clustered by-reference entries fetch nearby data pages, usually once each for a complete ordered scan.

An unclustered index yields sorted keys/RIDs but not physically sorted data records. Chasing every RID can require one random fetch per record. Compare that with a sequential file scan plus external sort, and check whether an index-only query avoids heap access. “Index provides order” alone does not establish that it is the cheapest plan.

PDF pp. 15–17

sections.title: Duplicate elimination and external hashing
sections.html:
DISTINCT and external hash partitioning

The source filters grade<90, projects cid, sorts and removes adjacent duplicates. Its retained course IDs are INFR-11011, INFR-10070, INFR-11122, INFR-11011; DISTINCT yields three IDs. Grouping equal values by hash can avoid global order when order is not required.

Partition into at most B−1 disk outputs using one input frame and hash hₚ. Rehash each partition in memory with an independent hᵣ: reusing only the partition hash would send everything to one local bucket. Oversized partitions can be recursively split, but repeated identical keys never separate under another key hash. DISTINCT/aggregation must collapse those duplicates or special-case the all-equal partition instead of recursing forever.

PDF pp. 18–22

Hash aggregation implementation

For each group key, look up its running state; create it if absent and update it otherwise. If states do not fit, spill partitions by group key and process them one at a time. All values of a group must reach the same partition.

The hash table, rather than just the partition’s raw bytes, must fit in memory: keys, counters, links and allocation overhead matter. In the source DISTINCT rehash table, INFR-11011 has multiplicity 2 while INFR-10070 and INFR-11122 each have 1. The earlier partitioning picture uses a different course-label instance; it illustrates routing, not a literal preceding state of this table.

PDF pp. 23–28

sections.title: Hash aggregation and memory requirements
sections.html:
Aggregate states and exact source averages

GroupState (count,sum)AVG
INFR-11011(2,155)77.5
INFR-10070(1,80)80
INFR-11122(2,145)72.5

AVG requires SUM and COUNT, not a running average alone. Combine partial groups by summing their sums and counts, then divide. MIN/MAX retain extrema, SUM a total, COUNT a count. Averages of unequal-sized partial groups cannot simply be averaged. SQL NULL handling must be incorporated in the chosen state updates.

PDF pp. 29–30

Memory threshold and sorting/hashing choice

With evenly sized B−1 partitions, raw partition size is N/(B−1). If its hash-state expansion factor is f>1, require approximately fN/(B−1)<B, so N<B(B−1)/f and B is on the order of sqrt(fN). Additional reserved frames tighten this budget.

The estimate fails under skew or large state overhead. Sorting gives useful global order and predictable merge passes; hashing often scales with distinct group count and can aggregate early. Neither the √N threshold nor “one or two passes” should be used without stating distribution, memory and output assumptions.

PDF pp. 31–32

quiz.question: For N=90 and B=6, how many I/Os does multiway sorting require when the final output is written?
quiz.explanation: Pass 0 reads and writes 90 pages and creates 15 runs. Five input frames plus one output frame merge them into 3 runs, then 1. These are three complete passes, each 90 reads+90 writes=180 I/Os: 3×180=540, including the final sorted-file write.
